summary: Programming-interruption research documents resumption costs, while LLM context studies show that longer context is not uniformly usable. Neither directly identifies when a coding-agent conversation should be reused, compacted or reset, so local telemetry remains essential.

items.text: Parnin and Rugaber (ICPC 2009) studied resumption strategies across more than 10,000 programming sessions from 85 programmers and document the cues developers use after interruptions; it supports explicit checkpoints but predates coding agents.

Two Sides of the Same Coin (2018) studies developer task switching through survey evidence and distinguishes benefits from disruption costs, offering adjacent evidence for task-similarity-aware switching policy.

Lost in the Middle (TACL 2024) shows that model use of relevant information varies with its position in long contexts; this supports monitoring context quality rather than assuming every retained token remains useful.

Programming by Chat (2026 preprint) analyzes 11,579 IDE sessions and provides recent descriptive evidence about conversational programming behavior; it is not a randomized comparison of reset policies.
